vignette:
Somchai was 69 and had spent most of his working life as a plumber, the kind of man who was used to crawling under houses, checking tight spaces, and trusting his hands to solve problems. He had emigrated from Southeast Asia decades earlier, built a quiet life in America, and now lived with his wife in a small house that he had carefully arranged so he could see the front door and the hallway from where he sat. It was in that ordinary domestic setting, and at work in basements and mechanical rooms, that the old fear kept finding him. He had been held captive years ago, and he spoke of it reluctantly, as if the words themselves might pull him back there. When he was unexpectedly alone with other men, or when a male coworker stepped too close in a narrow crawl space, his body would seize up before he could think. A wave of nausea could rise so quickly that he had to stop what he was doing, and a sharp pain in his neck would follow, making him stiff and watchful. Those moments taught Somchai to plan his movements around them: he began choosing seats near exits, lingering only briefly in crowded places, and checking ahead before he entered basements or mechanical rooms so he would not be caught off guard again. Those moments did not just remind him of the captivity; they seemed to carry the same menace, and Somchai had come to brace himself by planning an escape route before entering nearly any unfamiliar place, a habit that had become automatic over the years. He also avoided dates tied to the event, quietly withdrawing around anniversaries, and he described detaching himself from the memories as though he could place them at a distance and keep functioning.

What Somchai remembered was not a story he could tell in a straight line. He said the memories came back like a film that played over and over, each return feeling as vivid as the first time. To keep those scenes from breaking through, he began to avoid talking about them, to stay busy, and to plan his exits before he entered places where he might feel cornered. He had come to rely on those habits so completely that the memory never had a chance to be filed away; kept at a distance, it stayed intact and returned just as vivid and immediate whenever something resembled it. When he tried to explain what happened, he lost the thread and could not finish; the details seemed to break apart in his mouth, and he knew what happened without being able to find the words. Afterward, he tried to push the images away and keep himself busy, because once the scenes started looping in his head he found he could not settle until he was moving, distracted, or out of the room entirely. That very failure to speak made the memory feel more powerful, not less, because the event remained uncontained and alive in his mind. He could picture being confined with men he did not know, listening for footsteps, waiting for the next movement, and the images would cycle through his head until his stomach tightened and his neck went rigid. The replaying scenes made him dread not only the memory itself but anything that resembled it. A sudden motion from a man walking behind him in a supply store, a maintenance worker appearing in a doorway, even standing too close to another man in a parking lot could set him on edge immediately. The memory kept supplying these cues, and the cues kept dragging the memory back.

In response, Somchai had built a life around keeping the past at a distance, but the strategies had begun to narrow his world. He detached himself from the memories whenever they surfaced, telling himself not to dwell on them, yet the more he pushed them away the more they seemed to come back in fragments. He planned exits before entering restaurants, clinics, and hardware stores, and he monitored the men around him with a vigilance that left little room for comfort. Because he had never stayed with the thoughts long enough to make sense of them, they remained broken and sudden, returning to him just as sharply as before and catching him without warning. He had become on guard even inside his own home, checking the doors more than once and feeling his shoulders tense whenever he heard footsteps in the hall. The habit of avoiding anniversaries and slipping away from reminders did ease him for a moment, but it also kept the memory uncrossed and unspoken, so that when it returned it felt just as raw. At work, if he had to enter a cramped basement with another man, he would feel the old alertness surge and would calculate where he could move if he needed to get out quickly. His wife had noticed that he sat closer to the wall at gatherings and rarely stayed long. He no longer volunteered for some jobs that used to be routine, and he found himself making excuses to leave situations that involved being trapped in a space with men he did not know well.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was tired of living as if danger could appear at any moment. The fear was not only in his head; it came with nausea, neck pain, and a jolt through his whole body whenever something resembled the old captivity, and those reactions convinced him that he was still not safe. He had begun to worry that the memories and the constant guarding were wearing him down and making him less present with his wife and less confident at work. What brought him in was the sense that his world was shrinking around these reactions, and what he feared most was that he would never be able to talk about what happened clearly enough to make it feel over, or to stand in a room with other men without his body telling him he was back in that place again. The constant checking and retreating kept the danger feeling immediate in his body; if he needed that much preparation, he reasoned, then the world around him must still be unsafe.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows reminders and cues, but it does not clearly state that these triggers drive Somchai’s safety behaviors or avoidance as a causal response in the same paragraph.
The vignette describes intrusive memories, but it does not explicitly show the memories causing the use of maladaptive coping or avoidance behaviors in the same paragraph.
It states that he detaches, plans exits, and avoids reminders, but it does not clearly convey that these maladaptive strategies lead to more memory intrusions or fragmentation.
It describes safety behaviors and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that these strategies themselves increase his sense of threat or danger in a causal way.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows reminders and cues, but it does not clearly state that these triggers drive Somchai’s safety behaviors or avoidance as a causal response in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes intrusive memories, but it does not explicitly show the memories causing the use of maladaptive coping or avoidance behaviors in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: It states that he detaches, plans exits, and avoids reminders, but it does not clearly convey that these maladaptive strategies lead to more memory intrusions or fragmentation.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: It describes safety behaviors and vigilance, but it does not clearly state that these strategies themselves increase his sense of threat or danger in a causal way.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
